claims.claim: In a randomised trial of 327 adults aged 60 and over with insomnia and osteoarthritis pain, six 20 to 30 minute telephone sessions of CBT for insomnia over 8 weeks reduced insomnia severity more than education only, and at 12 months 56% versus 26% were in remission.
claims.supporting_passage: "This is a randomized clinical trial of 327 participants 60 years and older who were recruited statewide through Kaiser Permanente Washington from September 2016 to December 2018." ... "Six 20- to 30-minute telephone sessions provided over 8 weeks. Participants submitted daily diaries and received group-specific educational materials. The CBT-I instruction included sleep restriction, stimulus control, sleep hygiene, cognitive restructuring, and homework. The EOC group received information about sleep and OA." ... "Of the 327 participants, the mean (SD) age was 70.2 (6.8) years, and 244 (74.6%) were women. In the 282 participants with follow-up ISI data, the total 2-month posttreatment ISI scores decreased 8.1 points in the CBT-I group and 4.8 points in the EOC group, an adjusted mean between-group difference of -3.5 points (95% CI, -4.4 to -2.6 points; P < .001). Results were sustained at 12-month follow-up (adjusted mean difference, -3.0 points; 95% CI, -4.1 to -2.0 points; P < .001). At 12-month follow-up, 67 of 119 (56.3%) participants receiving CBT-I remained in remission (ISI score, ≤7) compared with 33 of 128 (25.8%) participants receiving EOC."
claims.location: Abstract: Design, Setting, and Participants; Interventions; Results
claims.pico_timeframe: Adults 60+ (mean 70.2) with moderate to severe insomnia and osteoarthritis pain, one US health plan / telephone CBT-I, 6 sessions over 8 weeks / education-only control (sleep and OA information) / Insomnia Severity Index; remission ISI 7 or less / 2 months and 12 months
claims.safe_wording: In a US trial of 327 people aged 60 and over who had both insomnia and arthritis pain, six phone sessions of CBT for insomnia (20 to 30 minutes each, over 8 weeks) improved sleep more than information about sleep and arthritis. A year later, 56 in 100 in the phone CBT group had no clinically significant insomnia, against 26 in 100 in the information group.
claims.qualifications: Everyone in the trial had osteoarthritis pain; one US health plan. The remission figures use the people with 12-month data (119 and 128), not all 327. Remission means a score of 7 or less on the Insomnia Severity Index. Pain improved after treatment but the difference was not sustained at 12 months.
claims.conflicting_or_uncertain: The comparator was education only. The trial did not compare telephone with app-based or face-to-face CBT-I, so the post must not imply the phone works better than an app. The abstract does not say whether the control group also had phone contact.

claims.claim: Telephone CBT-I needs only a phone for the sessions and was designed as an access route for people who lack ready access to insomnia treatment.
claims.supporting_passage: "Scalable delivery models of cognitive behavioral therapy for insomnia (CBT-I), an effective treatment, are needed for widespread implementation, particularly in rural and underserved populations lacking ready access to insomnia treatment." ... Key Points, Meaning: "Telephone CBT-I may improve access to an individualized and effective treatment for chronic insomnia among older persons with osteoarthritis pain, including those in rural and medically underserved areas."
claims.location: Abstract (Importance) and Key Points (Meaning), via PMC
claims.pico_timeframe: As for C11-09-a; the access claim is the authors' interpretation, not a measured outcome
claims.safe_wording: The therapy sessions in this trial were delivered by telephone. The researchers present phone delivery as a way to reach older people in rural and underserved areas who lack ready access to insomnia treatment.
claims.qualifications: The trial did not measure access or compare uptake between formats. Participants also kept daily sleep diaries and received written materials; how the diaries were returned is not stated in the abstract, so do not say 'nothing but a phone is needed'. Say 'the sessions were by phone'.
claims.conflicting_or_uncertain: Whether telephone CBT-I reaches people who are offline was not tested; it is a reasonable inference, which the post should present as the argument, not as a finding.

claims.supporting_passage: Discussion: "In contrast, comparable ELSA estimates (i.e., proportion of users of any frequency, aged 60 +) suggest that in England, this remained constant at 79% before and during the pandemic." | Results: "Weighted estimates from the nationally representative English Longitudinal Study of Ageing suggest that the prevalence of daily Internet use among adults aged 50 + in England increased from 52·9% in 2012/2013 (Wave 6), to 71·8% in 2018/2019 (Wave 9), and finally to 73·9% in June/July 2020" | "This discrepancy increased with age, with those aged 85 + being 17 percentage points less likely (or 22·1% relative to the June/July 2020 average) than those aged 50–64 to use the Internet daily." | Abstract: "Daily use in June/July 2020 was negatively related to age, neighbourhood deprivation, and loneliness, and positively related to partnership status, education, employment, income, and organisation membership." | Discussion: "It is also worth noting that older adults in care homes have been excluded by design. claims.conflicting_or_uncertain: The Ofcom figure the candidate suggested was not openable and is not used. Internet use among older people has been rising over time, so a 2020 figure may overstate current non-use slightly; say 'in 2020'.

claims.pico_timeframe: Adults with chronic insomnia disorder / behavioural and psychological treatments / GRADE-based recommendations
claims.safe_wording: The American Academy of Sleep Medicine advises against using sleep hygiene advice on its own to treat long-term insomnia. It recommends full CBT for insomnia, and suggests stimulus control, sleep restriction or relaxation therapy as single treatments.
claims.qualifications: The advice against sleep hygiene alone is a conditional recommendation ('we suggest ... not'), as are the single-component recommendations; only multicomponent CBT-I is a strong recommendation. Covers adults of all ages. Sleep hygiene can remain part of a multicomponent treatment.

claims.claim: In the HABIT trial in English general practice, four nurse-delivered sleep restriction sessions plus a sleep hygiene booklet reduced insomnia severity at 6 months more than the booklet alone, and were likely cost-effective.
claims.supporting_passage: "We did a pragmatic, superiority, open-label, randomised controlled trial of sleep restriction therapy versus sleep hygiene. Adults with insomnia disorder were recruited from 35 general practices across England and randomly assigned (1:1) using a web-based randomisation programme to either four sessions of nurse-delivered sleep restriction therapy plus a sleep hygiene booklet or a sleep hygiene booklet only." ... "we randomly assigned 642 participants to sleep restriction therapy (n=321) or sleep hygiene (n=321). Mean age was 55·4 years (range 19-88)" ... "At 6 months, mean ISI score was 10·9 (SD 5·5) for sleep restriction therapy and 13·9 (5·2) for sleep hygiene (adjusted mean difference -3·05, 95% CI -3·83 to -2·28; p<0·0001; Cohen's d -0·74)" ... "The incremental cost per QALY gained was £2076, giving a 95·3% probability that treatment was cost-effective at a cost-effectiveness threshold of £20 000."
claims.pico_timeframe: Adults 19 to 88 (mean 55.4) with insomnia disorder, 35 English general practices / 4 nurse sessions of sleep restriction + booklet / sleep hygiene booklet only / Insomnia Severity Index (0 to 28) / 6 months (also 3 and 12)
claims.safe_wording: In a large English general practice trial, the comparison group received a sleep hygiene booklet. People who also had four sessions of sleep restriction therapy from a practice nurse had less severe insomnia at 6 months (average score 10.9 against 13.9 on a 0 to 28 scale), and the treatment was likely to be good value for the NHS.
claims.qualifications: Not an older-adult trial: mean age 55 (range 19 to 88). Open label with a self-reported outcome. Pair with Buysse 2011 for older-adult evidence.

numbers.meaning: adults randomised (321 per group)
general practices in England
mean age and range in years
mean Insomnia Severity Index at 6 months, sleep restriction + booklet vs booklet only (lower is better; scale 0 to 28); adjusted difference 3.05 points
incremental cost per quality-adjusted life year gained (NHS and personal social services perspective)
probability the treatment was cost-effective at £20,000 per QALY

claims.claim: In older adults with chronic insomnia, brief behavioural treatment produced a response in 67% versus 25% with printed educational material (RCT).
claims.supporting_passage: "A total of 79 older adults (mean age, 71.7 years; 54 women [70%]) with chronic insomnia and common comorbidities were recruited from the community and 1 primary care clinic. Participants were randomly assigned to either BBTI, consisting of individualized behavioral instructions delivered in 2 intervention sessions and 2 telephone calls, or IC, consisting of printed educational material. Both interventions were delivered by a nurse clinician. The primary outcome was categorically defined treatment response at 4 weeks" ... "Categorically defined response (67% [n = 26] vs 25% [n = 10]; χ(2) = 13.8) (P < .001) and the proportion of participants without insomnia (55% [n = 21] vs 13% [n = 5]; χ(2) = 15.5) (P < .001) were significantly higher for BBTI than for IC. The number needed to treat was 2.4 for each outcome." ... "Improvements were maintained at 6 months."
claims.pico_timeframe: 79 older adults (mean 71.7) with chronic insomnia and comorbidities, Pittsburgh / brief behavioural treatment (2 sessions + 2 phone calls, nurse-delivered) / printed educational material / treatment response and no insomnia / 4 weeks (maintained at 6 months)
claims.safe_wording: In a trial of 79 older adults (average age 72) with long-term insomnia, about 2 in 3 improved after two nurse sessions and two phone calls of behavioural treatment, against 1 in 4 of those given printed information. The benefit was still there at 6 months.
claims.qualifications: Small single-centre US trial; the primary outcome was at 4 weeks. The printed information control is comparable to a leaflet but not identical to a sleep hygiene leaflet. Use 'about 2 in 3 vs 1 in 4' rather than n values, as group denominators are not stated in the abstract.
claims.conflicting_or_uncertain: No conflicting evidence identified; small sample means the size of effect is uncertain.

numbers.meaning: older adults randomised
mean age in years

number needed to treat for each outcome

claims.claim: CBT for insomnia is the recommended initial treatment for chronic insomnia in adults.
claims.supporting_passage: "ACP recommends that all adult patients receive cognitive behavioral therapy for insomnia (CBT-I) as the initial treatment for chronic insomnia disorder. (Grade: strong recommendation, moderate-quality evidence)."
claims.pico_timeframe: Adults with chronic insomnia disorder / CBT-I first / guideline
claims.safe_wording: The American College of Physicians recommends CBT for insomnia as the first treatment for long-term insomnia in adults.
claims.qualifications: US guideline, adults of all ages.

claims.claim: The trial randomised 291 adults aged 60 and over (mean 70.1) with insomnia and no current major depression to 2 months of CBT-I or sleep education therapy.
claims.supporting_passage: "This assessor-blinded, parallel-group, single-site randomized clinical trial assessed a community-based sample of 431 people and enrolled 291 adults 60 years or older with insomnia disorder who had no major depression or major health events in past year." ... "Participants were randomized to 2 months of CBT-I (n = 156) or SET (n = 135)." ... "Among 291 randomized participants (mean [SD] age, 70.1 [6.7] years; 168 [57.7%] female"
claims.location: Abstract: Design, Setting, and Participants; Interventions; Results
claims.pico_timeframe: Community adults 60+ with insomnia disorder, no current major depression or major health event in past year / CBT-I for 2 months / sleep education therapy (active comparator) / incident or recurrent major depressive disorder (DSM-5 interview) / up to 36 months
claims.safe_wording: The trial included 291 people aged 60 and over (average age 70) who had insomnia but were not depressed. They had 2 months of either CBT for insomnia or sleep education.
claims.qualifications: Single site in Los Angeles; people with a major health event in the past year were excluded.

numbers.meaning: people randomised (156 CBT-I, 135 sleep education)
mean age in years
treatment duration

claims.claim: Incident or recurrent major depression occurred in 12.2% of the CBT-I group and 25.9% of the sleep education group over follow-up (HR 0.51).
claims.supporting_passage: "Incident or recurrent major depression occurred in 19 participants (12.2%) in the CBT-I group and in 35 participants (25.9%) in the SET group, with an overall benefit (hazard ratio, 0.51; 95%, CI 0.29-0.88; P = .02) consistent across subgroups." ... "The findings of this randomized clinical trial indicate that treatment of insomnia with CBT-I has an overall benefit in the prevention of incident and recurrent major depression in older adults with insomnia disorder."
claims.pico_timeframe: As C11-28-a; outcome time to first major depressive episode; follow-up up to 36 months
claims.safe_wording: Over up to 3 years of follow-up, 12 in 100 people who had CBT for insomnia developed major depression, compared with 26 in 100 who had sleep education. The risk of depression over time was about half as high with CBT.
claims.qualifications: The 12 vs 26 in 100 are crude proportions of everyone randomised (19/156 and 35/135), not adjusted for unequal follow-up; the primary analysis was the hazard ratio of 0.51 (confidence interval 0.29 to 0.88, so the true reduction could be smaller or larger). Label icon arrays 'up to 3 years' and 'people randomised'. Do not use the 82.6% figure for CBT-I remitters: that compares a subgroup defined after randomisation and is not a randomised comparison.
claims.conflicting_or_uncertain: One trial, not yet replicated in the sources read. Sustained insomnia remission was modest in both groups (26.3% vs 19.3%).

sleep education group with incident or recurrent major depression, same period

claims.claim: Follow-up completion at 24 months was lower in the CBT-I group (73%) than the comparison group (87%); follow-up was extended from 24 to 36 months by protocol amendment; the sample was 83% White.
claims.supporting_passage: "The trial protocol was modified to extend follow-up from 24 to 36 months, with follow-up completion in July 2018." ... "7 [2.4%] Asian, 32 [11.0%] Black, 3 [1.0%] Pacific Islander, 241 [82.8%] White, 6 [2.1%] multiracial, and 2 [0.7%] unknown" ... "A total of 140 participants (89.7%) completed CBT-I and 130 (96.3%) participants completed SET (χ2 = 4.9, P = .03), with 114 (73.1%) completing 24 months of follow-up in the CBT-I group and 117 (86.7%) in the SET group (χ2 = 8.4, P = .004). After protocol modification, 92 (59.0%) of the CBT-I participants and 86 (63.7%) of the SET participants agreed to extended follow-up (χ2 = 0.7, P = .41), with 81 (51.9%) of the CBT-I participants and 77 (57.0%) of the SET group completing 36 months of follow-up"
claims.pico_timeframe: As C11-28-a
claims.safe_wording: Read it with care: it was one trial at one site, more than 8 in 10 participants were White, and more people dropped out of follow-up in the CBT group (73 in 100 completed 2 years, against 87 in 100 with sleep education). Only just over half completed 3 years.
claims.qualifications: Uneven drop-out could bias the result in either direction. Single site; excluded people with recent major health events, so frailer older people are under-represented.

completed 36 months of follow-up, CBT-I vs sleep education

claims.claim: A meta-analysis of 65 studies (3,577 people aged 5 to 102) found that in adults total sleep time, sleep efficiency and deep sleep fell and time awake after sleep onset rose with age, but only sleep efficiency continued to fall significantly after 60; age effects were modified, sometimes diminished, by how well participants were screened for illness, medicines and sleep disorders.
claims.supporting_passage: "65 studies representing 3,577 subjects aged 5 years to 102 years." ... "In adults, total sleep time, sleep efficiency, percentage of slow-wave sleep, percentage of REM sleep, and REM latency all significantly decreased with age, while sleep latency, percentage of stage 1 sleep, percentage of stage 2 sleep, and wake after sleep onset significantly increased with age. However, only sleep efficiency continued to significantly decrease after 60 years of age. The magnitudes of the effect sizes noted changed depending on whether or not studied participants were screened for mental disorders, organic diseases, use of drug or alcohol, obstructive sleep apnea syndrome, or other sleep disorders." ... "effect sizes for the different sleep parameters were greatly modified by the quality of subject screening, diminishing or even masking age associations with different sleep parameters."
claims.pico_timeframe: Healthy non-clinical people aged 5 to 102 / age / cross-sectional comparison across studies / polysomnography or actigraphy sleep measures / studies 1960 to 2003
claims.safe_wording: In healthy adults, sleep gets somewhat shorter, lighter and more broken with age. An older review of sleep studies found that after 60 only sleep efficiency (the share of time in bed spent asleep) kept falling clearly, and that age effects looked smaller when studies screened out illness, medicines and sleep disorders.
claims.qualifications: Do not paraphrase as 'most change has happened by 60': the abstract says only one measure continued to fall significantly after 60, which is not the same thing. Studies were mostly small and published 1960 to 2003.
claims.conflicting_or_uncertain: Boulos 2019 (larger, modern scoring) modelled a steady decline per decade across adulthood (see C11-14-b), so whether change levels off after 60 is uncertain.

numbers.meaning: size of the meta-analysis
age range in years
age after which only sleep efficiency continued to fall significantly

claims.claim: In healthy adults, measured sleep changes gradually with age: for each decade, total sleep time falls by about 10 minutes and time awake after sleep onset rises by about 10 minutes.
claims.supporting_passage: "Of 3712 articles, 169 studies, comprising 5273 participants, were eligible for inclusion." ... "For each decade of age, total sleep time decreased by 10·1 min (95% CI 7·5 to 12·8), sleep efficiency decreased by 2·1% (1·5 to 2·6), wake after sleep onset increased by 9·7 min (6·9 to 12·4), sleep onset latency increased by 1·1 min (0·3 to 1·9), arousal index increased by 2·1 events per h (1·5 to 2·6), percentage of N1 sleep increased by 0·5% (0·1 to 0·8), apnea-hypopnea index increased by 1·2 events per h (0·9 to 1·4)" ... "Changes with age in the percentage of N2 sleep (0·0%, 95% CI -0·1 to 0·1), N3 sleep (-0·1%, -0·1 to 0·0), and rapid eye movement (REM) sleep (0·0%, -0·1 to 0·0) were not significant."
claims.pico_timeframe: Healthy adult controls in sleep-laboratory studies (excluding people with conditions or treatments affecting sleep) / age per decade / meta-regression / polysomnography parameters / studies 2007 to 2016
claims.safe_wording: In healthy adults, a large review of overnight sleep studies found that each extra decade of age brought about 10 minutes less sleep and about 10 minutes more time awake during the night. That is a gradual, modest change, not a collapse of sleep.
claims.qualifications: Laboratory sleep of healthy volunteers; averages, not individual limits. Linear per-decade model; it does not show whether change speeds up or levels off in late life. Illustration: 40 years (for example 40 to 80) would be about 40 minutes less sleep on average, but only present this as arithmetic on the per-decade estimate if used at all.
claims.conflicting_or_uncertain: Partly differs from Ohayon 2004 (only sleep efficiency kept falling after 60); both agree the change in healthy people is modest.

numbers.meaning: size of the meta-analysis (healthy adults)
fall in total sleep time per decade of age
rise in time awake after first falling asleep per decade of age
fall in sleep efficiency per decade of age (percentage points of time in bed spent asleep)

claims.claim: The US National Sleep Foundation recommends 7 to 8 hours for older adults, against 7 to 9 hours for younger adults and adults.
claims.supporting_passage: "For teenagers, 8 to 10 hours was considered appropriate, 7 to 9 hours for young adults and adults, and 7 to 8 hours of sleep for older adults." ... "The recommendations reported here represent guidelines for healthy individuals and those not suffering from a sleep disorder. Sleep durations outside the recommended range may be appropriate, but deviating far from the normal range is rare."
claims.pico_timeframe: Healthy people without sleep disorders / expert consensus on appropriate sleep duration by age group
claims.safe_wording: An expert panel for the US National Sleep Foundation suggests 7 to 8 hours a night for older adults, against 7 to 9 hours for younger adults. So the saying that older people need less sleep is only slightly true: the recommended range drops by an hour at the top end, not at the bottom.
claims.qualifications: Consensus opinion, not measured need. The abstract does not state the age at which 'older adults' starts; do not write '65 and over' unless it is checked in the full text.

numbers.meaning: recommended nightly sleep for older adults (consensus)
recommended nightly sleep for young adults and adults (consensus)

claims.claim: Sleep complaints in older people are common and are associated with health problems such as depression, pain, respiratory symptoms, disability and medicines.
claims.supporting_passage: Foley 1995: "The frequencies of five common sleep complaints--trouble falling asleep, waking up, awaking too early, needing to nap and not feeling rested--were assessed in over 9,000 participants aged 65 years and older" ... "Less than 20% of the participants in each community rarely or never had any complaints, whereas over half reported at least one of these complaints as occurring most of the time. Between 23% and 34% had symptoms of insomnia" ... "In multivariate analyses, sleep complaints were associated with an increasing number of respiratory symptoms, physical disabilities, nonprescription medications, depressive symptoms and poorer self-perceived health. Sleep disturbances, particularly among older persons, oftentimes may be secondary to coexisting diseases." | Foley 2004: "Depression, heart disease, bodily pain and memory problems were associated with more prevalent symptoms of insomnia. Other conditions such as obesity, arthritis, diabetes, lung diseases, stroke and osteoporosis were associated with other sleep-related problems such as breathing pauses, snoring, daytime sleepiness, restless legs or insufficient sleep (<6 h nightly)." ... "These results suggest that the sleep complaints common in older adults are often secondary to their comorbidities and not to aging per se."
claims.pico_timeframe: Community-dwelling US adults 65+ (Foley 1995) and 55 to 84 (Foley 2004) / chronic conditions, mood, medicines / self-reported sleep complaints / cross-sectional
claims.safe_wording: Sleep complaints are common in later life, and in large US surveys they were linked with low mood, pain, heart and lung problems, disability and some medicines. The researchers concluded that much of the poor sleep seen in older adults goes with these conditions rather than with age itself.
claims.qualifications: Cross-sectional associations: they do not prove the conditions cause the poor sleep (the link can run both ways). US data from the 1980s and 2003.

numbers.meaning: people aged 65+ in Foley 1995
range across three communities with insomnia symptoms (Foley 1995)
adults aged 55 to 84 in the 2003 survey (Foley 2004)

claims.claim: New insomnia in later life mostly occurs alongside identifiable health or life factors: in a 3-year cohort of people aged 65 and over, only 7% of new cases occurred without associated risk factors, and nearly half of chronic insomnia remitted.
claims.supporting_passage: "Nearly 15% of the 4,956 participants without symptoms of insomnia at baseline reported chronic difficulty falling asleep or early morning arousal at follow-up, suggesting an annual incidence rate of approximately 5%. Incident insomnia was associated with depressed mood, respiratory symptoms, fair to poor perceived health, and physical disability." ... "Other factors associated with an increased risk of insomnia included use of prescribed sedatives, and widowhood. Only 7% of the incident cases of insomnia occurred in the absence of associated risk factors. Of the nearly 2,000 survivors with chronic insomnia at baseline, almost half no longer reported symptoms upon follow-up" ... "Because the vast majority of incident cases of insomnia were among persons with one or more of these risk factors, these data do not support a model of incident insomnia caused by the aging process per se."
claims.pico_timeframe: 6,899 US community residents aged 65+ / depressed mood, respiratory symptoms, poor health, disability, sedatives, widowhood / people without these / new self-reported insomnia / 3 years (1980s)
claims.safe_wording: In a large US study of people aged 65 and over followed for 3 years, only about 7 in 100 new cases of insomnia happened in people without a linked problem such as low mood, breathing symptoms, poor health, disability, sleeping tablet use or bereavement. Almost half of those with long-standing insomnia had improved 3 years later.
claims.qualifications: Observational and old (1980s US data); self-reported insomnia. The factors are linked with insomnia, not proven causes. Sedative use may be a response to insomnia rather than a cause.
claims.conflicting_or_uncertain: No conflicting evidence identified; the finding is consistent with Foley 1995 and 2004.

numbers.meaning: people aged 65+ in the cohort
people without insomnia at baseline who had it 3 years later (about 5% a year)
of new insomnia cases that occurred without any associated risk factor
people with chronic insomnia at baseline who no longer reported it 3 years later

claims.claim: Needing to pass urine at night (nocturia) is linked with insomnia in older adults.
claims.supporting_passage: "A total of 5396 older adults were included in the meta-analysis. The pooled estimate of the OR was 1.958 (95% CI: 1.609-2.384) for nocturia in patients with insomnia based on 7 studies in a random effects model" ... "The overall odds for nocturia in older adults is higher in patients with insomnia than those without and is associated with worse sleep outcomes." ... "A limiting factor of our analysis was the scarcity of available data, potentially causing an important selection bias."
claims.pico_timeframe: Older adults in 7 pooled studies / insomnia / no insomnia / nocturia (odds) / cross-sectional
claims.safe_wording: Getting up at night to pass urine is more common in older adults who have insomnia, and the two often go together, so it is worth asking about.
claims.qualifications: Association only; the direction is unclear (waking may prompt voiding, or the bladder may wake the person). Do not convert the odds ratio into 'twice as likely'. Small evidence base.
claims.conflicting_or_uncertain: Authors note scarce data and possible selection bias.

numbers.meaning: older adults in the pooled analysis

claims.claim: In healthy adults most age-related change in measured sleep has happened by about 60.
claims.supporting_passage: Ohayon 2004: "However, only sleep efficiency continued to significantly decrease after 60 years of age." | Boulos 2019: "For each decade of age, total sleep time decreased by 10·1 min (95% CI 7·5 to 12·8), sleep efficiency decreased by 2·1% (1·5 to 2·6), wake after sleep onset increased by 9·7 min (6·9 to 12·4)"
claims.pico_timeframe: As C11-14-a and C11-14-b
claims.safe_wording: Do not say 'most change has happened by 60'. Say instead that in healthy people sleep changes gradually with age, by about 10 minutes less sleep per decade, so a large or sudden change is not explained by age alone.
claims.qualifications: The candidate's paraphrase overstates Ohayon, and the more recent Boulos meta-analysis models a steady decline across adulthood.
claims.conflicting_or_uncertain: Two meta-analyses use different methods and eras; the plateau after 60 is uncertain.

claims.claim: In 1,280 people with polysomnography-confirmed idiopathic REM sleep behaviour disorder (mean age 66, 82.5% men), the rate of developing an overt neurodegenerative syndrome was 6.3% per year, and 73.5% had converted after 12 years.
claims.supporting_passage: "Idiopathic REM sleep behaviour disorder (iRBD) is a powerful early sign of Parkinson's disease, dementia with Lewy bodies, and multiple system atrophy." ... "We combined prospective follow-up data from 24 centres of the International RBD Study Group. At baseline, patients with polysomnographically-confirmed iRBD without parkinsonism or dementia underwent sleep, motor, cognitive, autonomic and special sensory testing." ... "Overall, 1280 patients were recruited. The average age was 66.3 ± 8.4 and 82.5% were male. Average follow-up was 4.6 years (range = 1-19 years). The overall conversion rate from iRBD to an overt neurodegenerative syndrome was 6.3% per year, with 73.5% converting after 12-year follow-up."
claims.pico_timeframe: People with polysomnography-confirmed idiopathic RBD at 24 specialist centres, no parkinsonism or dementia at baseline / prospective follow-up / Kaplan-Meier risk of parkinsonism or dementia (PD, DLB, MSA) / mean 4.6 years, up to 19
claims.safe_wording: Among 1,280 people whose dream enactment was confirmed as REM sleep behaviour disorder in specialist sleep centres, about 6 in 100 a year went on to develop Parkinson's disease, dementia with Lewy bodies or a related condition. By 12 years the estimate was about 3 in 4.
claims.qualifications: Specialist-centre patients with sleep-study confirmation, mostly men; the 12-year figure is a Kaplan-Meier estimate (average follow-up was 4.6 years). It is not a personal prognosis for everyone who acts out dreams; people reporting dream enactment in the community are much less likely to have confirmed RBD (see C11-21-f). Conversion outcomes include Parkinson's disease, dementia with Lewy bodies and multiple system atrophy.
claims.conflicting_or_uncertain: Individual risk varies widely; the paper lists predictors (motor, smell, cognition and others). A sleep study is needed to confirm RBD.

numbers.meaning: people with confirmed idiopathic RBD, 24 centres
mean age in years
men
average follow-up (range 1 to 19)
rate of developing an overt neurodegenerative syndrome
estimated proportion converted by 12 years (Kaplan-Meier)

claims.claim: REM sleep behaviour disorder is a core clinical feature in the consensus diagnostic criteria for dementia with Lewy bodies.
claims.supporting_passage: "RBD is now included as a core clinical feature because it occurs frequently in autopsy-confirmed cases compared with non-DLB (76% vs 4%). It often begins many years before other symptoms, may become less vigorous or even quiescent over time, and should be screened for using a scale that allows for patient or bed partner report." ... "If the PSG shows REM sleep without atonia in a person with dementia and a history of RBD, there is a ≥90% likelihood of a synucleinopathy,sufficient to justify a probable DLB diagnosis even in the absence of any other core feature or biomarker"
claims.location: Full text: Core clinical features, REM sleep behavior disorder; Indicative biomarkers
claims.pico_timeframe: People with dementia being assessed for DLB / RBD history / autopsy-confirmed DLB vs non-DLB / consensus criteria
claims.safe_wording: Acting out dreams (REM sleep behaviour disorder) is one of the four core features used to diagnose dementia with Lewy bodies. It often starts many years before other symptoms.
claims.qualifications: The 76% vs 4% compares autopsy-confirmed DLB with other dementias; it is not the chance that someone who acts out dreams has DLB.

numbers.meaning: RBD frequency in autopsy-confirmed DLB vs non-DLB cases
likelihood of a synucleinopathy when a sleep study shows REM sleep without atonia in a person with dementia and an RBD history

claims.claim: RBD is often reported by the bed partner; conditions that mimic it (such as severe obstructive sleep apnoea) must be excluded, and doubt should prompt referral to a sleep clinic or polysomnography.
claims.supporting_passage: "RBD is a parasomnia manifested by recurrent dream enactment behavior that includes movements mimicking dream content and associated with an absence of normal REM sleep atonia. It is particularly likely if dreams involve a chasing or attacking theme, and if the patient or bed partner has sustained injuries from limb movements." ... "should be screened for using a scale that allows for patient or bed partner report.Conditions mimicking RBD are common in people with dementia, e.g., confusional awakenings, severe obstructive sleep apnea, and periodic limb movements, all of which must be excluded by careful supplementary questioning to avoid a false-positive diagnosis. If there is any doubt whether a sleep disturbance is due to RBD, referral to a specialist sleep clinic should be made, or polysomnography (PSG) requested."
claims.location: Full text: Core clinical features, REM sleep behavior disorder
claims.pico_timeframe: People being assessed for DLB; consensus guidance
claims.safe_wording: Ask the bed partner as well as the person: dreams with a chasing or attacking theme and injuries from movements in sleep make REM sleep behaviour disorder more likely. Other problems can look similar, including severe sleep apnoea, so if there is doubt, refer for a sleep study.
claims.qualifications: Written for DLB assessment; the principle (partner history, exclude mimics, sleep study if doubt) applies generally. Access to sleep studies varies; do not imply everyone will get one quickly.

claims.claim: Injuries to the person or bed partner occur, and bedroom safety measures are recommended.
claims.supporting_passage: AASM 2023, Good Practice Statement: "It is critically important to help patients maintain a safe sleeping environment to prevent potentially injurious nocturnal behaviors. In particular, the removal of bedside weapons, or objects that could inflict injury if thrown or wielded against a bed partner, is of paramount importance. Sharp furniture like nightstands should be moved away or their edges and headboard should be padded. To reduce the risk of injurious falls, a soft carpet, rug, or mat should be placed next to the bed. Patients with severe, uncontrolled RBD should be recommended to sleep separately from their partners, or at the minimum, to place a pillow between themselves and their partners." | McKeith 2017: "if the patient or bed partner has sustained injuries from limb movements"
claims.location: AASM abstract (Good Practice Statement); McKeith full text
claims.pico_timeframe: Adults with RBD / bedroom safety / expert consensus
claims.safe_wording: US sleep specialists advise making the bedroom safe: remove objects that could hurt someone, move or pad sharp furniture and the headboard, put a soft rug or mat beside the bed, and, if episodes are severe, sleep apart or put a pillow between partners.
claims.qualifications: Good practice statement based on expert consensus, not trial evidence.

claims.claim: Antidepressants can bring on or worsen REM sleep behaviour disorder, so medicines should be reviewed; but antidepressant-associated RBD can still be a sign of early neurodegeneration.
claims.supporting_passage: AASM 2023: "Adult patients with drug-induced RBD" ... "9. * The AASM suggests that clinicians use drug discontinuation (vs drug continuation) for the treatment of drug-induced RBD in adults. (CONDITIONAL)" | Haba-Rubio 2018: "Compared with RBD- participants, RBD+ took more frequently antidepressants and antipsychotics (23.8% vs. 5.4%, p = .005; 14.3% vs. 1.5%, p = .004, respectively)" | Postuma 2013: "Compared to matched controls, RBD patients taking antidepressants demonstrated significant abnormalities of 12/14 neurodegenerative markers tested" ... "However, on prospective follow-up, RBD patients taking antidepressants had a lower risk of developing neurodegenerative disease than those without antidepressant use (5-year risk = 22% vs. 59%, RR = 0.22, 95%CI = 0.06, 0.74)." ... "Development of RBD with antidepressants can be an early signal of an underlying neurodegenerative disease."
claims.location: Abstracts: AASM recommendations; HypnoLaus Results; Postuma 2013 Results and Conclusions
claims.pico_timeframe: Adults with RBD (AASM); general population 1,997 (HypnoLaus, cross-sectional); 100 specialist-centre iRBD patients, 27 on antidepressants (Postuma 2013, prospective)
claims.safe_wording: Some medicines, including antidepressants, are linked with acting out dreams, and sleep specialists suggest stopping the drug where it is thought to be the cause. But in one specialist cohort, people whose symptoms came with antidepressants still showed early signs of Parkinson-type disease, so a medicines review should not end the assessment.
claims.qualifications: The link in the general population is an association (people with RBD took antidepressants more often). The specific classes (for example serotonergic drugs) were not verified from the text read; say 'some antidepressants'. Do not use the 'up to 6% of users' figure, which is background in the Postuma 2013 abstract. Stopping an antidepressant needs its own risk-benefit decision.
claims.conflicting_or_uncertain: Postuma 2013 is small and single-centre; 5-year risk was lower with antidepressant-associated RBD (22% vs 59%) but not zero.

numbers.meaning: antidepressant use in people with vs without confirmed RBD, general population (HypnoLaus)
5-year risk of neurodegenerative disease, RBD with vs without antidepressant use, specialist cohort of 100

claims.claim: Dream enactment reported in the community often turns out not to be RBD on a sleep study, so the specialist-centre conversion figures cannot be applied to everyone who acts out dreams.
claims.supporting_passage: "Full polysomnographic data from 1,997 participants (age = 59 ± 11.1 years, 53.6% women) participating in a population-based study (HypnoLaus, Lausanne, Switzerland) were collected." ... "Three hundred sixty-eight participants endorsed dream-enactment behavior on either of the two MUPS questions, and 21 fulfilled polysomnographic criteria for RBD, resulting in an estimated prevalence of 1.06% (95% CI = 0.61-1.50), with no difference between men and women."
claims.pico_timeframe: General population adults (mean age 59), Lausanne / questionnaire dream-enactment report / home polysomnography / RBD diagnosis / cross-sectional
claims.safe_wording: In a Swiss population study, 368 of about 2,000 adults said they acted out dreams, but only 21 had REM sleep behaviour disorder on a sleep study. About 1 in 100 adults had it. A report of dream enactment is a reason to assess, not a diagnosis.
claims.qualifications: One city; mean age 59, so younger than many geriatric patients. Screening was by two questionnaire items. 21 of 368 is roughly 1 in 18, but present the raw numbers rather than a derived ratio unless needed.

numbers.meaning: adults with home polysomnography
reported dream-enactment behaviour on a questionnaire
met polysomnography criteria for RBD
estimated prevalence of RBD in this population

claims.claim: Discussing what RBD may mean (risk disclosure) is valued by patients and professionals, but individual prognosis is uncertain.
claims.supporting_passage: "For healthcare professionals, the main obstacles include uncertainty in formulating individualized prognoses, ethical challenges linked to the principle of beneficence and concerns about the possible emotional impact of disclosure. From the patients' viewpoint, there is a clear need for comprehensive and robust information about their condition, even though obtaining accurate and trustworthy sources can be difficult. Risk disclosure is considered essential by both patients and professionals, but a systematic step-by-step approach has yet to be implemented for people with iRBD on progression to neurodegenerative diseases."
claims.pico_timeframe: Patients with isolated RBD and professionals; 8 studies; attitudes to risk disclosure
claims.safe_wording: A recent review found that both patients and professionals see discussing future risk as essential, while professionals find it hard to give an individual prognosis. The conversation needs time, honesty about uncertainty, and follow-up.
claims.qualifications: Small scoping review (8 articles). The recommendation to have a careful, supported conversation is an ethical judgement and should be written as one ('we should').

candidates.reason: The trial evidence is solid: McCurry 2021, 327 adults aged 60+ with insomnia and osteoarthritis pain; six phone sessions; at 12 months 67/119 (56%) vs 33/128 (26%) in remission against education only. CBT-I as first-line is supported (ACP 2016, AASM 2021). Internet non-use is supported for England from ELSA (Kung and Steptoe 2023): 79% of people aged 60+ used the internet at all in 2020, so about 1 in 5 did not, and daily use fell with age and deprivation (care homes excluded). The NICE Sleepio claim could not be verified and must go. The angle's premise that digital CBT-I widens access for many people was not sourced. The trial did not compare phone with app delivery. Diaries and written materials were also used, so 'a phone is all you need' overstates the evidence.
candidates.revised_angle: Who gets left out: the recommended first treatment for long-term insomnia is CBT, but any route to it that needs the internet misses many older people: in England in 2020 about 1 in 5 people aged 60 and over living at home did not use the internet at all, and daily use was lowest in the oldest age groups and more deprived areas. A US trial showed CBT for insomnia works when the sessions are held by phone: a year later 56 in 100 older adults had no significant insomnia, against 26 in 100 given information only. Close with a question to ask the GP practice ('Can I have CBT for insomnia by phone or in person?'). Optionally add that an English trial (HABIT) showed practice nurses can deliver sleep restriction therapy in four sessions. Do not claim phone beats apps, do not name NICE, and do not state that the NHS routinely offers phone CBT-I. If apps are mentioned, do not make claims about how widely apps are used or how well they work; no source for that was checked in this batch.

candidates.reason: All essential claims are supported. AASM 2021 conditionally advises against sleep hygiene as a single treatment and recommends multicomponent CBT-I (strong), with stimulus control, sleep restriction and relaxation suggested as single components (conditional). HABIT (Kyle 2023): in 35 English practices, the comparison group got the booklet, and four nurse sessions of sleep restriction gave ISI 10.9 vs 13.9 at 6 months, at £2,076 per QALY. HABIT's mean age was 55 (19 to 88), so Buysse 2011 must carry the older-adult evidence: 79 people, mean age 71.7, response 67% vs 25% with printed information, maintained at 6 months.

The core idea is supported, but not the 'most change by 60' framing. Ohayon 2004 says only sleep efficiency kept falling after 60, and the larger, modern Boulos 2019 meta-analysis models a steady change of about 10 minutes less sleep and 10 more minutes awake per decade in healthy adults. NSF gives 7 to 8 hours for older adults against 7 to 9 for adults (the age cut-off is not in the abstract). Foley 1999 is the strongest source for the angle: only 7% of new insomnia in people aged 65+ occurred without an associated factor (low mood, breathing symptoms, poor health, disability, sedatives, widowhood), and almost half of chronic insomnia remitted within 3 years. Foley 1995/2004 and Verbakel 2023 support the checklist of linked problems (pain, mood, breathing, heart disease, medicines, night-time urination) as associations.
candidates.revised_angle: Test the saying fairly: the recommended range for older adults is 7 to 8 hours against 7 to 9 for younger adults, so the saying is slightly true. In healthy people sleep changes slowly, by about 10 minutes less sleep and 10 minutes more time awake per decade. A marked or new change is usually not age alone: in a large study of people over 65, only 7 in 100 new cases of insomnia happened without a linked problem such as low mood, breathing symptoms, poor health, disability, sleeping tablets or bereavement. Visual: 'What ageing explains' (slightly shorter, lighter, more broken sleep) vs 'What to check' (pain, low mood, breathing pauses or loud snoring, needing the toilet at night, medicines, recent loss); credit Boulos 2019 and Foley 1999. Drop the 'by about 60' opening and use associative wording (linked with, not caused by).

candidates.reason: All essential claims are supported. Postuma 2019: 1,280 people with polysomnography-confirmed iRBD at 24 centres, mean age 66, 82.5% men; conversion 6.3% a year and an estimated 73.5% by 12 years. RBD is a core DLB feature (McKeith 2017; 76% vs 4% at autopsy), screened by patient or bed-partner report, with mimics including severe sleep apnoea, and referral or polysomnography if in doubt. AASM 2023 gives the bedroom-safety good practice statement and suggests stopping the drug in drug-induced RBD. Antidepressants are linked with RBD (HypnoLaus 23.8% vs 5.4%), but antidepressant-associated RBD can still signal neurodegeneration (Postuma 2013). HypnoLaus also shows that only 21 of 368 people who reported dream enactment had confirmed RBD, which supports the judge's caveat. Say that the 73.5% comes from confirmed specialist-centre patients and is not a personal prognosis. Schedule apart from C08-17.

All essential claims are supported by the Irwin 2022 abstract. 291 adults aged 60+ (mean 70.1) without depression; CBT-I vs sleep education for 2 months. Depression over up to 36 months: 19/156 (12.2%) vs 35/135 (25.9%), HR 0.51 (0.29 to 0.88). Limitations: one site, 82.8% White, follow-up extended from 24 to 36 months by protocol amendment, 24-month completion 73.1% vs 86.7%, and only 52% to 57% completed 36 months. Label the icon arrays 'up to 3 years, crude proportions of those randomised'. Do not use the 82.6% remitter figure (non-randomised comparison).
